The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • South Africa’s health officials at the launch in June of lenacapavir, a drug that provides strong protection against HIV when administered twice a year.Credit: Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty.
  • It has been revealed that earlier this month, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a generic version of the HIV drug lenacapavir for use as a preventive treatment.
  • A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

South Africa’s health officials at the launch in June of lenacapavir, a drug that provides strong protection against HIV when administered twice a year.Credit: Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a generic version of the HIV drug lenacapavir for use as a preventive treatment. Twice-yearly injections of this game-changing medicine — originally developed by the tech giant Gilead Sciences in Foster City, California — have been shown to be more than 95% effective at preventing HIV acquisition1. At the same time, as Nature reports in a News feature, an HIV vaccine — that would ultimately be a more robust solution to preventing HIV — is closer than ever before.

A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies.

A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies.

In 2024, Gilead signed licensing agreements with six pharmaceutical companies, allowing them to make and sell generic versions of lenacapavir in 120 low- and middle-income countries, subject to regulatory approval. The recent FDA approval brings access a step closer in these countries. The cost to users has been set at US$40 per year, fuelling hopes that the drug will help to bring the global HIV epidemic under control.

It has been revealed that these welcome developments contrast with the situation of public funding for HIV research and treatment, which is reeling from deep and unconscionable cuts from the US government. Many of the researchers whom Nature spoke to for the News feature had been funded by a programme for preclinical HIV-vaccine research run by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). But the agency ended the programme last year, forcing researchers to scale back their research and seek alternative funding. Whatever funding comes next is likely to be less stable and less predictable than the NIH funding. It’s imperative that the cuts be reversed — or new government funding sources found.

Recent findings suggest that the path to an HIV vaccine has been long and bumpy, with decades of high-profile and costly failures, but there is now light at the end of the tunnel. The latest strategy — known as germline targeting — is designed to trigger the production of rare, highly potent antibodies that can prevent infection with diverse HIV strains. The technique has shown encouraging results in animal models2–4 and in early trials in humans5. Researchers are more optimistic than they’ve been in years that an effective HIV vaccine could be on the horizon.

The end of AIDS is in sight: don’t abandon PEPFAR now.

The end of AIDS is in sight: don’t abandon PEPFAR now.

But in the meantime, antiretroviral drugs such as lenacapavir look poised to have a major impact on infection prevention. In Africa alone, newly introduced infections could be cut by around one-third if just 5% of adults most likely to acquire HIV received the drug, and by half if it was given to one-fifth of adults, according to the Gates Foundation’s Institute for Disease Modelling in Seattle, Washington.

In a recent development, but lenacapavir alone is unlikely to bring the HIV epidemic fully under control. There are several reasons for this: first, it’s not always easy to determine who needs the drug most. Second, to be effective, the drug must be taken for most of someone’s life — or at least while they are sexually active. Third, even $40 a year is unaffordable for people on the very lowest incomes.

Until recently, the United States was the stand-out funder for antiretroviral drugs for people living with HIV in low-and middle-income countries. That stopped in January 2025, when the US administration suspended funding. Although it later restored a limited amount, the effects have been devastating. A survey published earlier this year found that some 1,700 facilities previously offering treatments to people living with HIV had closed as a result (see go.nature.com/4a7ftp4).

Sources indicate that trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Industry observers note that such instability highlights the importance of vaccines. “The funding cuts that happened in the past couple of years have really made it even more obvious how fragile that system of reliance” on drug access is, claims Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Disease in Johannesburg. And that fragility, as Rogier Sanders, an HIV-vaccine researcher at Amsterdam University Medical Centre, says, is why research into a vaccine remains a priority: “A vaccine makes you independent from access to drugs.”.

But the US cuts have not only curtailed the preclinical vaccine programme, they have also forced the postponement and scaling back of an HIV vaccine trial in South Africa. They have also affected supporting research, such as surveillance efforts tracking HIV evolution in African countries, claims Nairobi-based Vincent Muturi-Kioi, who is leading development of HIV vaccines at the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative in Newly introduced York City.

According to recent reports, success stories such as the repurposing of lenacapavir as a preventive treatment and progress in vaccine development show the importance of investment in health. It is imperative that HIV vaccine research and deployment continues to receive support, at the same time as rolling out lenacapavir as widely as possible.

It could take more than a decade to translate the encouraging results with germline targeting into an effective HIV vaccine, and the current strategy might encounter more hurdles.

It has been revealed that the world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine and has a drug capable of preventing infections. Now is the time for funders to ramp up investment, not cut it back.

Zeki Çelik was withdrawn from Türkiye's starting line-up in Bordeaux after feeling tightness in the same left thigh muscle he injured in October. With Pierre Kalulu already sidelined, Juventus face tests that could leave them without both main right-sided defenders for Venezia and Omonia.

Zeki Çelik’s international week ended before kick-off in Bordeaux. The Juventus full-back was named in Türkiye’s starting line-up for Sunday’s Nations League match against France. His left hamstring tightened up as he went through the warm-up. He was taken out of the matchday squad as a precaution. Barış Alper Yılmaz started in his place.

An Emirhan Topçu own goal and a goal from Eli Junior Kroupi put France ahead. Abdülkerim Bardakcı scored a late reply for Türkiye. The result left France top of Nations League Group A1 with 13 points. They are through to the quarter-finals, which are due next March.

It has been revealed that çelik now returns to Turin for tests at J|Medical. Those results will decide how Juventus line up at the back after the international break.

The location is what worries Juventus. Çelik was substituted at half-time in the 2-2 Europa League draw with Rennes. His scans took place on the morning of Friday 23 October. He began a rehabilitation programme straight away and was expected back after the November break.

Tuttosport counted him among Spalletti’s first returning players, alongside Vicario and Gatti. The paper placed the Bordeaux problem in the biceps femoris of his left thigh. That is the same area as the October injury.

Çelik had only just returned after weeks out. That is why the warm-up incident has raised fears of a relapse. No diagnosis has yet been confirmed.

Juventus were already without Pierre Kalulu. He picked up the injury in the game against Fiorentina. He began treatment and was withdrawn from the France squad. Sky Sport Italia expected him to be out for about three weeks. That would rule him out of both the Venezia and Omonia matches.

If Çelik’s problem proves to be a relapse, Spalletti could be without both of his main right-sided defenders for those two games. The schedule offers little room for recovery. The Omonia match is the second of four games in 12 days.

The league position adds pressure. After 11 rounds Juventus are seventh in Serie A with 18 points. Their record reads five wins, three draws and three defeats.

Venezia visit Turin first, at 12:30 on 22 November in round 12 of Serie A. Omonia then come to the Allianz Stadium at 21:00 on 26 November in the Europa League league phase.

Chelsea transfer news: Xabi Alonso wants Barcelona right-back Jules Koundé at Chelsea and is ready to sell Marco Palestra, his £47m summer signing, to make room, according to El Nacional. The outlet states Alonso has pushed the case, a claim it credits to FourFourTwo, and that Palestra has Serie A interest from Juventus, AC Milan and Napoli, though it mentions no bid.

Barcelona would reportedly listen to offers of around €50m, roughly £43m, because Hansi Flick doesn’t treat Koundé as untouchable. The 28-year-old has started three of six LaLiga games this season after an ankle sprain on 17 October kept him out for over a month. El Nacional calls him a backup behind Eric García and notes he’d welcome the move.

Koundé completes 93.9% of his passes, wins 58.8% of his duels and has 58 France caps, a composed defender who could play right-back or on the right of a back three. His body is the worry: a hamstring problem in March, then an ankle injury that lingered.

Palestra won Serie A’s Defender of the Year award at Cagliari, and his 81 completed dribbles topped every defender in Europe’s top five leagues. A thigh injury delayed his Chelsea debut until October, and El Nacional puts him at 202 minutes across six matches. Alonso prefers Josh Acheampong at right-back and, per BBC Sport, uses Palestra from the bench before Malo Gusto. He scored once in 37 league games, and his crossing remains modest.

Recent findings suggest that not as a swap. Palestra is a wing-back who beats opponents on the outside, while Koundé is a passer and cover defender best placed on the right of three centre-backs. Selling one doesn’t remove the need for the other, and Chelsea’s real shortage is right-sided cover: Reece James is injured and has been used in midfield, and Acheampong, a centre-back by trade, is filling in at right-back.

Koundé would solve that, but Gusto is the sale to make. He has lost his place, is reportedly open to a January exit, and Chelsea priced him at £75m in June, so even a discounted fee would cover much of Koundé’s £43m.

Sources indicate that selling Palestra after 202 minutes would mean writing off a player Alonso recruited and said needs time to adapt, to buy a 28-year-old with a muscle-injury record. Chelsea were fifth, 11 points behind Arsenal, before Leeds visited, without European football. Buy Koundé if the medical is clean, sell Gusto and keep Palestra.

Liverpool transfer news: Liverpool are tracking Borussia Dortmund left-back Daniel Svensson, according to fussball-news.de, which names them and Arsenal as the most interested clubs.

Manchester United, Leeds, Milan, Juventus, Inter and Real Madrid are also watching the 24-year-old. Liverpool and Milan are reportedly preparing concrete steps for the winter window, although the report attributes no bid to either.

Dortmund will not make it easy. They want to keep a player contracted until June 2029 and initiative to raise his salary, while Svensson feels settled and has no wish for a rushed move. A sale would cost at least €45m (about £38m), and Premier League clubs are ready to test Dortmund with a €30m (roughly £25m) offer, yet FotMob values him at just €23m.

In a recent development, the numbers explain the interest. Svensson has started all 10 Bundesliga games this season. His expected assists total of 1.13 comes without a single assist, and he has made 22 tackles, 14 interceptions and 45 recoveries while passing at 86.1%. He can play in midfield.

The flaws are clear. He has won only eight of 29 aerial duels and landed six of 32 crosses. He also plays as a wing-back in front of a back three, so Andoni Iraola’s back four would ask him to defend more of the flank alone.

It has been revealed that iraola’s 4-2-3-1 sends full-backs forward, and Milos Kerkez, bought for a reported £40m last year, has no goals or assists in the Premier League this season. Kostas Tsimikas, 30, is the backup on a contract that expires next year.

In a recent development, not in January, and not at €45m. A €30m offer would fail, and £38m for a player FotMob values at €23m is poor business. Summer 2027 is the realistic window, once Tsimikas’s deal has run down.

In a recent development, the bigger problem sits on the other flank. Ronald Araujo, a centre-back by trade, is filling in at right-back while injuries have hit that position all season, so Iraola needs a natural right-back more urgently than a second left-back. Kerkez is 22 and signed until 2030, so Svensson would challenge him rather than replace him, which is healthy given Kerkez’s lack of end product.

It has been revealed that kerkez arrived with two Premier League seasons behind him, while Svensson would have to adapt to a newly introduced league and a new system. Liverpool should buy a right-back first and hold a ceiling of around £35m for Svensson, because above that they would repeat the Kerkez gamble with less evidence.

Breaking: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hate long-haul flights?
  • Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m.
  • NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 rolled out, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

In a recent development, that's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Sources indicate that but you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," notes Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

According to recent reports, the spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

Sources indicate that but if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

The sides had contrasting fortunes in their most recent league outings as the hosts fell to a 4-1 defeat against PSV Eindhoven, while the visitors came from behind to beat 10-man Willem II.

Off the back of managing just one win in 11 matches across September and October, NEC have made a strong start to November, winning three of their four games in all competitions. Their latest success was Thursday’s 3-1 triumph over Ligue 1 side Rennes.

The Eniesee’s only defeat since the turn of the month came at home to PSV on Saturday when a slow first-half display saw them go into the interval down by three, and there was hardly any room for a resurgence after the break.

Dick Schreuder's men are 12th in the Eredivisie table and remain within touching distance of teams right now in the drop zone, which highlights how underwhelming their league campaign has been compared to last season’s unprecedented success.

With no wins in any of the last five encounters, recent matches against Twente do not hold happy memories for NEC, who are seeking a first victory since January 2024 to avoid suffering consecutive league defeats for the first time this season.

Recent findings suggest that yet to keep a clean sheet in 2026-27, Sunday’s hosts have plenty of room for improvement defensively. A shutout this weekend would be a good starting point, particularly against opponents who have scored 11 times across the last five meetings.

Twente are averaging three goals per game across their six away league outings - thanks in no small part to November 1’s 9-0 demolition of SBV Excelsior - this season, so NEC’s issues at the back will definitely be music to their ears. However, the Enschede-based outfit did come up short in their last assignment on the road.

Days after coming back for a third game running en route to a 2-1 win over Willem II, Twente looked set to secure another positive result from behind in Thursday’s Conference League clash against Freiburg, where they trailed initially but managed to level proceedings through Younes Taha, only for Jan-Niklas Beste to net a stoppage-time winner.

That ended a six-match winless run for the Tukkers, and they will now seek to get back to winning ways, having not lost back-to-back competitive matches since July.

Like NEC (12/21), John van den Brom’s men have scored most of their goals (19/32) after half time, hinting that this weekend’s clash could come to life as it progresses, so supporters should not be in a hurry to leave if it proves a slow burner.

With their title rivals scheduled to be in action earlier, Sunday’s visitors risk losing crucial ground if they fail to claim maximum points in the final fixture of matchday 14.

FC Twente form (all competitions):.

Bram Nuytinck and Philippe Sandler are confirmed defensive absentees for NEC, while Emre Mor is also unavailable for Sunday’s match.

Perr Schuurs has missed the last three games and remains a major doubt, so Ahmetcan Kaplan is likely to marshal the defence once again.

Bryan Linssen has netted four times across his last three home matches for the hosts, and the 36-year-old will be aiming to deliver once again.

Max Bruns, Krzysztof Kurowski, Filip Erik Thorvaldsen, Lars Unnerstall, and Thomas van den Belt will miss the trip to Nijmegen as Twente continue to contend with injury problems.

Sondre Orjasaeter has registered a goal contribution in both of his two appearances for Twente against NEC and will be keen to extend that run.

Crettaz; Bras, Kaplan, Fonville; Kers, Nejasmic, Lebreton, Bakker; Chery, Tadic, Linssen.

FC Twente possible starting lineup:.

Drommel; Adelgaard, Nijstad, Propper, Van Rooy; Weidmann, Zerrouki; Orjasaeter, Taha, Rots; Weghorst.

Both teams have scored in four of the last five meetings between Twente and NEC, suggesting a clean sheet for either side may be unlikely on Sunday.

However, Twente possess greater quality across the pitch and should have enough to claim all three points.

In a recent development, tottenham transfer news: Tottenham Hotspur are one of four clubs tracking Hakan Calhanoglu, according to Tuttomercatoweb. The Italian outlet lists Galatasaray, Juventus and Como alongside Spurs, although it gives no detail on how far Tottenham’s interest has progressed.

The timing matters because the Inter midfielder’s contract expires on 30 June 2027, which lets him agree a pre-contract with a foreign club from January. Inter want to extend but are trimming wages for their over-30s. Calhanoglu earns roughly £5.7m a year, and Inter are discussing £4.4m plus bonuses. He prefers to stay but hopes to avoid a heavy cut, and no formal offer exists yet.

Industry observers note that calhanoglu turns 33 in February. FotMob demonstrates three goals in 485 minutes from nine Serie A appearances, 91.4% pass accuracy, 20 chances created and a 98th-percentile ranking for shot attempts among Serie A central midfielders.

In a recent development, passing range, long-distance shooting and dead-ball quality remain his strengths. He wins only 44.4% of his duels, though, completes a quarter of his dribbles, and his recovery speed will keep dropping with age. FotMob values him at about £6.4m, down from a £39m peak in 2024.

Roberto De Zerbi wants his midfield to dictate play from deep, which suits Calhanoglu’s skills. Spurs have 15 points from 11 league games after beating Ipswich 2-0 on Saturday, their fourth win in five. Yet Sandro Tonali (£100m) and Mateus Fernandes (£85m) joined in July, and Rodrigo Bentancur, Conor Gallagher and Archie Gray compete for the same places.

Industry observers note that not as a priority. Money isn’t the obstacle. Tonali reportedly earns more than £275,000 a week, so Calhanoglu’s wages would barely register, and a free transfer costs no fee. Squad space is the problem. Spurs bought Tonali and Fernandes to run De Zerbi’s base for years, and a 33-year-old in the same role would either sit on the bench or take minutes from Gray and Lucas Bergvall, whom the club needs to develop.

Spurs would also struggle to sell the project without European football, while Galatasaray can reportedly offer higher wages. The case only strengthens if Tonali or Bentancur leaves, or if De Zerbi wants a penalty and set-piece specialist. Neither applies now, and nothing forces Spurs to act in January.

Calhanoglu’s output is real, but it comes with a decline in athleticism that a 33-year-old can’t reverse. Spurs would be paying for a short-term fix in a position where they have already invested £185m in the long-term answer.

"We were not able to control and attack the game in the way we want," Haaland told TNT Sports. "Football is easy and difficult.

“When you win it's easy and you know what to do. When you don't you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think, but it's not so easy.

"We have so much quality so it's about getting the quality out in every player. We have to regroup, stay positive and bring energy on the pitch and try to do our best.".

According to recent reports, speaking at a press conference on Friday, Maresca said: "I think Erling is a winner. It's normal that he's not happy when we don't win games but not just Erling, everyone.

"Remember just a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch. You can write and think many different things.

"Erling is upset. I'm upset because we're not winning games. But this is our job, this is football. That's why I need to maintain the balance.".

Asked if Haaland’s mood affect his performances, with some social media clips showing him visibly frustrated on the pitch, Maresca replied: "I think he gesticulates when we were winning games, and not receiving balls.

Recent findings suggest that "He's a nine. They live day by day for goals and winning games. If they don't score or win games they're upset. So I don't think that affects his game, but for sure he's not happy not winning games but everyone is on the same page.".

“Again, a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch, he was dancing in training. He's happy. It's normal that results affect the mood, that's why we need to win games, but I don't see any problem at all with Erling.".

With Man City sitting six points behind Arsenal at the top of the Premier League table and in danger of falling further behind in the title race, Maresca has made it clear that his team will “try our best” to win at the Emirates Stadium.

Haaland will relish another battle with Arsenal, having scored in six of his previous eight Premier League meetings with the Gunners, netting in each of his last four such games.

Manchester United will launch a upcoming matchday mental health and suicide prevention initiative at Saturday’s game against Brentford at Old Trafford.

Industry observers note that rhys Bennett, who was the captain of United's last FA Youth Cup-winning team in 2022, has spoken about the benefits of a recent Talk About It Mate session at Salford Lads Club. Bennett’s father David tragically took his own life last year.

‘It’s probably the most powerful thing I’ve ever done,’ said Bennett. ‘I’ve never done anything like this before. It’s made me feel even better than I did when I came in the door two hours ago. I’ve enjoyed every minute of it.

Recent findings suggest that ‘My dad passed at 51 and I think he grew up in the, “you’ll be alright, just crack on” (generation). He was an honest working man, and he went about his daily business until it became too much for him.

Industry observers note that ‘For him it would have been a really crucial thing to get things off his chest. A judgement free zone. It would have helped him massively. People are sharing the same experiences, people sat in a circle all going through different things.

Manchester United will launch a fresh matchday mental health and suicide prevention initiative at Saturday’s game against Brentford at Old Trafford.

Rhys Bennett (right), who was the captain of United's last FA Youth Cup-winning team in 2022, attended a recent Talk About It Mate session at Salford Lads Club.

In a recent development, ‘To be honest, I was a little bit nervous. I'm not a nervous kind of person, but I think within five minutes, it's just no judgment and having that full confidence in being able to talk about how I'm really feeling.

Industry observers note that ‘I'm coming up for a year of my dad's passing. My dad committed suicide, and I played football for a living. I think it's hard navigating through being in a high-pressure environment.

According to recent reports, ‘I think it is the judgment thing, and not wanting to burden other people. But I think it's so key that you realise that most of the time it's not a burden.’.

According to recent reports, bennett, who made a permanent move to Fleetwood in the summer and played in the League Two club’s shock Carabao Cup win over Arsenal last month, added: ‘You put the brave face on, and I feel weaker. But the more I talk about it, and the more I let my emotions out, that definitely does make me stronger in day-to-day life.

‘I used to just shut it out because I'm rocking up on a Saturday and a Tuesday in front of fans, and I've got to perform, and I feel everything. You get the adrenaline and everything of a football match, and then I'm back down to square one.

According to recent reports, ‘Just how open everyone was and how open I could be myself, really did surprise me. There wasn’t at any point that I couldn’t share something I was feeling. Everything came from the heart, it was really authentic and really powerful.’.

Running five weekly men’s groups across Salford and with more than 1,000 group sessions delivered, Talk About It Mate creates spaces where men can connect, share experiences and support one another.

With a community-led approach to improving mental health and well-being, the organisation helps men build connections and reduce isolation.

United will host 10 sessions of The Check-In this season aimed at providing a welcoming space where supporters can drop in to talk with trained counsellors and volunteers.

Bennett, whose father David tragically took his own life last year, spoke about how the session gave him 'full confidence in being able to talk about how I'm really feeling'.

Man United say their partnership with Talk About It Mate will provide a welcoming space where supporters can access help on matchdays.

Mike Richard, founder of Talk About It Mate, said: ‘We've spent years creating spaces where men feel safe enough to open up, and we're proud to be working with Manchester United to bring that approach to supporters.

‘Football has an incredible ability to bring people together, but being surrounded by thousands of people doesn't necessarily mean you feel connected. We know that some of the most notable conversations can start in ordinary, familiar places – that's the kind of environment we want to create at Old Trafford.

‘This isn't about waiting until someone reaches crisis point. It's about making conversations around mental health a normal part of everyday life.’.

According to The Samaritans, 5,738 suicides were registered in England in 2025, which equates to 11.1 deaths per 100,000 people.

The male suicide rate was 17.2 per 100,000 – compared to 5.4 per cent among females – with men aged 50-54 having the highest rate of any population group.

Rachel Fraser, United’s internal communications and inclusion director, noted: ‘Our fans give so much to this club, and ensuring they feel supported in return is incredibly important to us.

‘Through our partnership with Talk About It Mate, we are proud to provide a welcoming space where supporters can access help on matchdays.

Sources indicate that ‘Football creates friendships and communities for fans that span generations. The Check-In builds on that sense of connection and seamlessly fits into the matchday routine, providing a safe and accessible space for those needing support.’.

By Naim Beneddra | 27 Nov 2026 18:19.

As Everton prepare to welcome Liverpool to the Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday, one former Toffees midfielder has recalled the unfortunate sequence of events that prevented him from experiencing the Merseyside derby during his time in English football.

Orel Mangala, who spent the 2024-25 season on loan at Everton from Lyon, was denied the opportunity to participate in the final derby at Goodison Park after severe weather forced the original fixture to be postponed and a serious knee injury subsequently ended his season.

Now playing in Spain with Getafe on loan from Lyon, the Belgium international continues to follow his former club and has been impressed by the progress made under David Moyes.

The Belgian had been due to face Liverpool on December 7, 2024, but the fixture was called off on safety grounds as Storm Darragh swept across the United Kingdom.

Sources indicate that by the time the rearranged match came around, Mangala's season was already over. The midfielder had suffered an anterior cruciate ligament injury during Everton's 1-0 victory over Brighton & Hove Albion on January 25.

"I missed one of the derbies because of a storm. The match was postponed and then I tore my cruciate ligament, so in the end I couldn't play in it," Mangala recalled in an interview with Top Mercato.

What made the circumstances particularly unfortunate was that the rearranged fixture on February 12, 2025, became one of the most memorable occasions in Goodison Park's recent history.

James Tarkowski's spectacular stoppage-time equaliser secured a 2-2 draw for Everton, ensuring that the Toffees avoided defeat in the final Merseyside derby at their home of more than 130 years.

Although Mangala never experienced the rivalry on the pitch, the 28-year-old had already witnessed its significance in the city, describing the atmosphere in the build-up to the fixture and the sense of anticipation among supporters.

Mangala has kept a close eye on Everton's fortunes since returning to Lyon, and he believes the club's encouraging start to the current campaign is a reflection of the foundations laid over the past few seasons.

The Toffees have collected 16 points from their opening 11 Premier League fixtures and sit seventh in the table, with Liverpool five points ahead in fourth place.

Mangala highlighted the emergence of 19-year-old midfielder Harrison Armstrong, whom he knew during his time at Everton, and expressed his satisfaction at seeing the club competing in the top half of the table.

The Belgian also praised Everton's infrastructure and suggested that their improvement had come as little surprise to him given what he had witnessed during his season on Merseyside.

Sources indicate that recent history nevertheless illustrates the scale of the challenge facing Moyes's side on Sunday. Everton have won only two of their last 31 Premier League meetings with Liverpool, although 14 of those encounters have ended in draws.

Andoni Iraola's men have won the last three editions of the derby, including a 2-1 victory on their first visit to the Hill Dickinson Stadium in April.

Everton will therefore be looking to record their first derby victory at their new home on Sunday, having last beaten Liverpool in April 2024 at Goodison Park.

For Mangala, the fixture offers another opportunity to follow a rivalry whose significance he came to appreciate during his brief spell on Merseyside, even though circumstances never allowed him to experience it as a player.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

Industry observers note that the atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

Recent findings suggest that this was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he mentioned. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the strategy. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

Sources indicate that “As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the initiative disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”.

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

It has been revealed that if they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight latest signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

Sources indicate that A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

Sources indicate that there was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

In a recent development, everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

Recent findings suggest that A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

Recent findings suggest that this is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

According to recent reports, it was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

Sources indicate that he did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

For Newcastle, a win tonight would take them up to seventh, just two points behind Chelsea in fourth. Despite the heavy away defeats and unconvincing performances, that would be an impressive start for a new manager. Matthias Jaissle has already felt the full force of the contrasting emotions on Tyneside in his three months in charge but substantial questions hang over his team. In particular, the “vertical football” style he brought from the Red Bull coaching school in Germany.

In a recent development, A defeat tonight, coming so soon after the 3-1 defeat in the Carabao Cup to Everton, will intensify the criticism of his approach. It would also suggest Newcastle, despite all their positive talk over the summer, are nothing more than a mid-table team who will be looking over their shoulders rather than upwards this season.

A win for Everton will have the same uplift for David Moyes at Everton, also taking them up to seventh in the table. Given all the problems attached to their summer recruitment - or rather the lack of it - Everton will have defied the grim pre-season predictions heading into the second international break. The table is starting to take shape and so are the narratives around every club.

Industry observers note that juventus president Gianluca Ferrero set out the leadership's view of the rebuild at the Brussels launch of the club's European Union fan club. He spoke while a capital raise of about €200m is open and a UEFA settlement limits spending.

Juventus president Gianluca Ferrero went to Brussels on 18 November with a clear message for supporters. Restoring the club to its former self is its absolute ambition, he said, adding that the club is following the path set out by its chief executive and is confident this can happen. He spoke at the opening of the Juventus Official Fan Club European Union, which is chaired by MEP Sandro Gozi. The timing gives the statement weight.

The newly introduced supporters’ club opened at the Iosono il Piemonte event space. Its stated purpose is to link Juventus supporters with the institutional centre of Europe.

In a recent development, before the opening, the delegation went to the European Parliament with Gozi. Chief Club Affairs Officer Giorgio Chiellini led the group alongside Ferrero. Piedmont regional president Alberto Cirio attended the opening, as did MEPs who have joined the fan club.

The visit showed Chiellini’s work on the club’s relations with institutions and European football. It also gives supporters an official club in Brussels.

The financial backdrop is demanding. Juventus posted a consolidated loss of €66m for 2025/26. On 12 November, the board approved the offer, using part of the €250m authority granted by shareholders at the extraordinary meeting on 3 November.

Industry observers note that the offer involves up to 208.5m new shares at €0.96 each. Shareholders can buy one new share for every two they hold. The price is 28.36% below the theoretical ex-rights price, based on that day’s share price. The remaining €50m of the authority can be used in later financial years, depending on the club’s financial needs and investment prepares.

Industry observers note that the spending limits come from UEFA. European football’s governing body fined Juventus €20m for breaking the football earnings rule. Of that amount, €14m is conditional. The club agreed a three-year settlement with annual targets. It also faces limits on registering fresh players on its UEFA List A.

According to recent reports, those are the limits within which Ferrero’s ambition must be pursued. Any improvement in the squad has to fit within the annual targets agreed with UEFA.

Subscription rights can be traded on Euronext Milan until 25 November, and the offer closes on 1 December 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, mentioned it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also confirmed his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo noted the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed.".

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

Recent findings suggest that he has been facing growing criticism since pitching a proposal of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the blueprint but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 27 Nov 2026 18:24, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 18:25.

Gil Vicente will look to strengthen their position in the top half of the Primeira Liga table when they welcome struggling Estoril Praia to Estadio Cidade de Barcelos on Sunday evening.

Also in contention for a European place, the hosts sit seventh in the Primeira Liga table, two points behind fifth-placed Arouca, while the visitors are bottom of the standings and hoping a change in management can spark a revival.

Since replacing Cesar Peixoto in the summer, Luis Pinto has done a decent job of maintaining Gil Vicente's push to end a four-year wait for European football after the club narrowly missed out last season, finishing sixth in the table.

Pinto has guided the side to 18 points from their opening 11 league fixtures (W5, D3, L3), with their campaign built around a solid defence that has conceded the joint second-fewest goals in the division (eight), although their 10 scored is the second-lowest tally among teams outside the bottom three.

Os Galos  have alternated between winless spells and encouraging runs throughout the season, but the Barcelos club head into this encounter on the back of consecutive victories after going three matches without taking full spoils.

A 3-1 success over Olhanense at the weekend saw the Roosters advance to the last 16 of the Taca de Portugal, where they will face Braga, with that cup success following a 2-1 win away to Santa Clara, a result which marked Gil’s third consecutive league victory on the road.

However, their home form has taken a dip, with Pinto's men, who won their first two matches in Barcelos this season, failing to take maximum points in each of their last four top-flight outings on their own turf (D2, L2), while also drawing a blank in the most recent two.

Meanwhile, Estoril could hardly have made a worse start to the season, with the Praia club the only side yet to record a victory in the division, having managed just two draws from 10 league matches, although they have a game in hand against Maritimo.

Much of the Canarinhos' struggles have stemmed from a blunt attack that has found the net a league-low five times, while they have also conceded 19 goals, and their problems at both ends of the pitch were further exposed in a 4-0 defeat to leaders Porto in their most recent top-flight outing.

Estoril's woes were compounded at the weekend when they suffered a 3-2 loss to second-tier side Felgueiras, with disciplinary problems proving costly as Ricard Sanchez, Xeka and Samuel Amissah were all sent off.

The result also brought an end to Sergio Raimundo's short spell in charge after he replaced Vasco Matos in October, and Joao Giao has been appointed as the third manager of the Praia club this season following his earlier spell at Nacional.

Interestingly, Giao's only league victory during his four-match spell at Nacional came against Estoril, although supporters of the Canarinhos can take some encouragement from the fact that their side have won two of the last three meetings with Gil, including a 3-1 success when the teams met in February.

Gil  are monitoring the fitness of Marvin Elimbi, who is close to recovering from an injury but was not considered ready to feature in the Taca de Portugal victory over Olhanense.

Hector Hernandez made a substitute appearance last time out after missing the previous six matches through fitness problems and could be given more minutes on Sunday as he looks to regain full match sharpness.

Mohamed Bamba also came off the bench in that encounter to make his first appearance for Gil after a 10-month layoff through injury, giving the hosts another option in midfield.

However, Arthur Tchaptchet remains a doubt, having yet to feature for the Roosters this season due to physical discomfort.

With domestic suspensions carrying over into the league, Xeka, Sanchez and Amissah will all miss Sunday's match following their red cards against Felgueiras.

The visitors will also be without Isra Salazar and Fabricio Garcia, who are recovering from ruptured cruciate ligaments, leaving Giao with limited options as he prepares for his first match in charge.

Yanis Begraoui returned from a muscle injury with a substitute appearance against Felgueiras and scored from the penalty spot, making him a likely starter here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 27 Nov 2026 18:38, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 18:42.

After coming close to a rare away win in England, Napoli will return to their ailing domestic campaign on Sunday, when they visit Serie A strugglers Sassuolo.

The Partenopei pushed Manchester City hard in the Champions League, but they are still facing an early European exit; meanwhile, their hosts face a long fight for top-flight survival.

Despite coming within minutes of victory in Manchester, where they drew 2-2 with Man City on Tuesday night, Napoli are still sitting inside the Champions League’s elimination zone with only three games left to play.

Following their league-phase exit last season, more continental misery could await for the Partenopei, who are also performing below expectations in Italy’s top flight.

Napoli have made their worst start to a league campaign since 2007 - when they were newly promoted - and even after last week’s 1-0 win over Torino they lie eighth in the Serie A standings.

Under Massimiliano Allegri, who replaced Scudetto winner Antonio Conte in the summer, the Campanian club have won just six of their 17 fixtures and are yet to record consecutive wins.

Before heading to Reggio Emilia, history suggests they can finally do so on Sunday: Napoli have lost just one of 12 away games against Sassuolo in Serie A.

Having won each of the last three while scoring 10 goals, they will be strong favourites with the best in-play betting sites.

In fact, such has been Napoli’s dominance at any venue, Sassuolo have lost the last seven league meetings by a staggering aggregate score of 23-2.

That should cause concern for fans of the Neroverdi, as they are yet to keep a clean sheet this season and presently have the worst defensive record in Serie A.

Seven decades have passed since any side avoided relegation after conceding at least 30 goals within 12 matchdays, so the Emilian club already have a mountain to climb.

Despite firing Alberto Aquilani and hiring Roberto D’Aversa during the last international break, they failed to benefit from a ‘newly introduced-manager bounce’ when losing 2-0 to Genoa last weekend.

So, Sassuolo have now lost all of their last six games - including three on home turf - leaving them stuck inside the drop zone.

Napoli form (all competitions):.

Following his emotional return to England, Kevin De Bruyne is set to miss Sunday’s game with muscle fatigue, joining Napoli’s long absence list. Alex Meret, Benoit Badiashile, Alisson Santos, Stanislav Lobotka, Alessandro Buongiorno and Antonio Vergara were already unavailable, while captain Giovanni Di Lorenzo has resumed full training but may not be risked.

Rasmus Hojlund and Scott McTominay were also back in Manchester on Tuesday night, and they must share the burden in the absence of top scorer De Bruyne.

Meanwhile, Sassuolo's talisman will be present at the Mapei Stadium: Domenico Berardi has scored three league goals versus Napoli since making his Serie A debut against them back in 2013.

Each of those strikes were on home turf - though the most recent was during the 2020-21 season - and Berardi should join Sebastiano Esposito and Armand Lauriente in the hosts’ trident attack.

D’Aversa switched to a back three on his dugout debut, but it remains to be seen if that experiment will continue this weekend.

Vasilje Adzic has undergone surgery after suffering a knee injury against Genoa, joining Cristian Volpato, Daniel Boloca, Fedde Leysen and Ismael Kone on the sidelines.

Sassuolo possible starting lineup:.

Muric; Walukiewicz, Idzes, Cande; Van der Brempt, Thorstvedt, Matic, Obrador; Berardi, Esposito, Lauriente.

Napoli possible starting lineup:.

Milinkovic-Savic; Beukema, Rrahmani, Marin; Politano, Anguissa, Gilmour, McTominay, Olivera; Lang; Hojlund.

The pressure is all on Napoli to beat free-falling Sassuolo, who last won in September and are still searching for an elusive clean sheet.

It may not be pretty, but the Partenopei should eventually prevail, given their greater firepower and experience.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a bell ringing in the Underground.

The copper-line page phone in Shaft #4 is going off, but it takes a minute for any of the miners to notice. They’re too busy dealing with a tunnel collapse and subsequent break in the geothermal line servicing Sectors 51–57.

It’s late morning, as measured by the water clocks and those who swear by them. It’s midnight, as determined by the Moon and stars, cavorting a few thousand feet above their heads. But the oldest miner on this crew is 60, which is about 30 years too young to remember stars or moons, or appreciate the difference between morning and night.

This is one reason why the Mona Lisa Lottery, so loved by the old-timers, fails to stir up the same excitement it used to. Too intent on repairs, the miners forget that the annual drawing is scheduled for today.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, the ringing registers and curiosity calls them away from their work. Headlamps bob up and down in the dark. The sound of axes and drills drops off sharply, save for one stubborn miner still working, right below a rock face chiselled with the encouraging-but-long-false words: This Way Out.

It has been revealed that they gather round the ringer box and the foreman hushes them before pressing the phone tight to one ear, cupping his free hand over the other. Every noise echoes tenfold in the tunnels, and the foreman has to ask the voice on the other end to repeat themselves.

“Abel?” the foreman repeats. “Are you sure?”.

A few miners huff wry laughs at the name, muttering, “Of course it’s him.”.

The foreman looks around, failing to find the lucky winner among his workers, “Well, where is he?”.

A couple outstretched thumbs and jerks of the head give the foreman his answer, unmistakably directed towards the only pickaxe still singing in the dark.

No one can opt out of the Mona Lisa Lottery. No one can give away their ticket to someone else.

Sources indicate that but Abel’s tempted to decline the honour. He’s got work to do. And climbing up 2,000 feet to wait in line with the other winners for hours, all to stare at a square 30-by-21 inches for 5 whole minutes, doesn’t seem like a good use of his time.

It’s only Adèle, the old woman in the cave next door, who convinces him to make the trek upstairs.

Adèle was ten when the evacuations happened. She’s now two months shy of being a proper centenarian. Her mind isn’t as sharp as it used to be. She can’t remember what she had for breakfast, but she remembers the horrors they descended from well enough, all those lines of desperate people sent down below with canned goods, heirloom seeds and not much else.

Sources indicate that the treasures preserved from the Old World are few and Abel’s been given the chance to see one of the last. Arguably, the best. If she wasn’t blind as a bat, Adèle might kill him for his ticket. If she didn’t love him like a son, that is.

“Don’t be a fool,” she tells him plainly. “Go see what you’ve been missing.”.

Recent findings suggest that the journey to the higher levels snakes up ladders and through tight squeezes, skirting the underbelly of the Safe Zone. There’s a breath of strange breeze up here, not conjured by any air machines. It makes some winners too nervous and they abandon the wait, rushing back down the way they came.

According to recent reports, abel’s not afraid. But he still thinks it’s a waste of time.

Adèle warned him that the wait for the Mona Lisa was just like this. When she was eight, her family waited for two hours just to get a glimpse. It doesn’t make sense to him. He doesn’t understand how a mere painting could be worth the trouble.

In a recent development, he’ll never know. Because that’s not what the Mona Lisa Lottery is all about. Despite the name, Abel’s not queuing for oil paint on a poplar panel.

The Mona Lisa is not in the Underground. They couldn’t waste the limited space. Leonardo’s lady still sits in the crumbling ruins of her museum gallery, her half-smile gone grimmer these days. She’s lonely without visitors. A wild boar passed her way a decade before, searching for truffles in the jungles of the overgrown Louvre. No one’s been by since.

She sighs into her patient smile; she waits with folded hands. Ever the optimist, she thinks her friends may return someday.

Tifos are back at the Emirates. Those loud, passionate designs which last season galvanised Arsenal en route to a first Premier League title in 22 years return on Sunday for the visit of Manchester City.

An emotionally-charged fixture between the title holders and the team found guilty of the majority of 115 breaches of the league's financial rules by an independent commission (which is being appealed by Man City) awaits.

Still, it can be revealed that Sunday's display will be more restrained than initially considered.

Recent findings suggest that daily Mail Sport understands that a supporter-led group, established by the Arsenal Advisory Board (AAB) last season, initially raised an idea with Arsenal of referencing Man City's charges in the tifo. However, following consultation with the club, collectively the idea was dropped.

Recent findings suggest that instead the tifo will be done 'in the Arsenal way to inspire the fanbase', a source says. They added: 'It will galvanise and charge the fans in the right way.'.

According to recent reports, these matters can often be delicate. For example, it's understood a debate was had over the north London derby tifo ahead of Arsenal vs Tottenham in November 2025 at the Emirates, which involved a montage of club icons from past and present. And at the very top, positioned deliberately, sat Sol Campbell.

Sol Campbell, perched atop this Arsenal tifo for the derby game against Tottenham last season, moved between the clubs in a highly contentious transfer in 2001.

What Arsenal offered on that PSG night in 2025 caused embarrassment – a solitary white cannon on a red backdrop.

Recent findings suggest that his 2001 move from Spurs to the Gunners remains one of the rivalry's deepest fault lines. Arsenal initially thought it could be too provocative but proceeded as the group were adamant on the imagery.

The reception when the tifo unveiled was immediate. The players felt it. The supporters felt it. Thierry Henry himself shared the image on social media with a simple verdict: 'What a tifo! Thank you, Gooners!'.

It has been revealed that as revealed in the book 22 Years: The Inside Story of Arsenal's Title-Winning Season, later in the season Mikel Arteta met up with the creators to say thank you and gifted each of them a signed, framed picture of the Tottenham tifo. Stuart MacFarlane, the club's chief photographer, was also there to take pictures of the group alongside Arteta. The Spaniard privately values the energy these displays create and embraces them.

It's understood Arteta checks the tifo designs before they are finalised. Much work goes into creating them, as reflected in the final proposal for Sunday's tifo which had to be confirmed and sent to the manufacturers nearly three weeks before matchday.

It has been revealed that the artwork is printed on a square shape canvas which is then cut out and backed onto a paper-like material. That is cable-tied to a huge rectangular netting and tied to the roof with further cables and ropes.

The design along with the attached apparatus weighs around a couple of hundred kilograms, which is a serious amount. The lightweight fabric also has to be fire retardant and meet weight restrictions.

The work involved in putting the tifo together has seen volunteers invited to the Hale End academy this Friday to cable tie the tifo and get the design laid out on an indoor pitch.

Recent findings suggest that budgets have to be met, too, for the group are allocated an undisclosed amount to cover tifos for the whole season. Blowing the budget on one or two displays would rule out further spectacles later in the season.

It has been revealed that the latest design builds on a growing trend which Arsenal began to grasp just over a year ago, the mission to properly create tifos initially starting in April 2025. Arsenal had unveiled their own tifo ahead of a Champions League semi-final first leg against Paris Saint-Germain — the first to be draped from the Emirates Stadium's roof in the arena's history.

For those confused by the term 'tifo', it stems from the Italian word tifosi, meaning passionate supporters. The designs are an attempt to galvanise fans, building an atmosphere with powerful messaging and provocative imagery to unsettle opponents.

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta checks the tifo designs before they are unveiled.

Mikel Arteta noted he hopes Manchester City's guilty verdict for breaching Premier League financial rules does not overshadow Sunday's crunch clash against Arsenal.

In a recent development, man City were found guilty of the large majority of charges for breaking the league's financial regulations between 2009 and 2018, in a period which saw them win eight trophies. The Manchester club insist they're innocent and are appealing the independent commission's verdict.

When asked about whether the charges will overshadow the match, Arteta remarked: 'I hope that it doesn't because it's a process that is still open, it's not resolved and I don't know what is going to happen.

'I think when we have two teams at the level that they both are at right now with the quality players that are on that pitch, it's a massive game and a big game to enjoy.'.

It has been revealed that he added: 'That (the match) is the only thing that we should put the energy and the focus in. There's nothing else.'.

Meanwhile, Arteta mentioned there is a chance David Raya will be fit enough to play on Sunday.

Raya appeared to be in agony as he was forced off in the 70th minute of Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle last Saturday, hurting his left shoulder in an accidental collision with William Osula.

There were initial fears the goalkeeper could be facing an extended spell on the sidelines, with Kepa Arrizabalaga playing in Tuesday's Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund.

Arteta stated: 'We still have a few hours before the game. We're still trying to get everyone back.'.

On if there's 'a ray of hope' that Raya will be available, he added: 'Yeah.'.

In a recent development, what Arsenal offered on that PSG night was widely mocked – a solitary white cannon on a red backdrop. That was it. A sterile design for one of the biggest European nights the Emirates had ever hosted, at that time.

It's understood a club-produced design had been used over a fan-led alternative, mainly because there was limited time between the proposal and the game itself.

The episode proved to be a pivotal turning point, led by the AAB.

The AAB is the club's formal fan-engagement body, created in 2021 following the backlash over Arsenal's involvement in the wretched European Super League plot — a breakaway competition set to feature 12 of Europe's leading clubs. The subsequent supporter anger forced Arsenal to improve their communication with fans.

After the PSG tifo disappointment, the AAB helped create a new group for the start of the 2025–26 season focused on creating tifos. Arsenal wanted to learn from the error, and this was their way of putting fans back in control.

Recent findings suggest that it's worked. The outcome resulted in a slew of eye-catching displays in the previous campaign from Campbell to Leandro Trossard's eye-goggles celebration for the 'history in our sights' tifo ahead of the Champions League quarter-final second leg against Sporting Lisbon — or the 'over land and sea' design with a huge ship for the semi-final second leg against Atletico Madrid.

By softening the parameters and letting fan representatives into the inner sanctum, Arsenal have utilised a marginal gain Arteta had craved ever since he took charge seven years ago — make the Emirates a fortress.

While there was an initial temptation from the AAB to reference Man City's guilty verdict in Sunday's tifo, the overall message will be unmistakably clear: Arsenal are now in charge.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

In a recent development, VC stated that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

According to recent reports, "The ball is now in the employer's court," VC noted in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, stated it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 newly introduced cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC noted it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

According to recent reports, the ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

Sources indicate that the ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger stated the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, declared aims to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl noted on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck.".

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he remarked.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support.".

In a statement issued after the announcement of the intends, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement noted.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it mentioned.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the looks, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he remarked, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals.".

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius revealed on Tuesday.

He remarked that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius remarked in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously unveiled, as well as latest radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also noted that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He remarked Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and newly introduced transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents.".

It also mentioned that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank.".

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission mentioned stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 newly introduced businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR mentioned the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also noted that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

Aims confirmed by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the initiative, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law.".

Meanwhile, more upcoming businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

Since the arrival of Spanish head coach Carlos Vicens to replace the departed Paulo Fonseca in early November, Lyon have kept back-to-back clean sheets, winning 1-0 at Lille in Ligue 1 last weekend before a draw in the Europa League on Thursday night.
