📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 14:08 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 14:14 EST, 27 November 2026.

On the website of Pluto Data Analytics, prospective clients are given a taste of what they can expect if they form a partnership with the London-based firm.

Under a section headed ‘Transferability You Can Trust,’ football clubs are told: ‘At Pluto, we use advanced machine learning to validate how a player might adapt in a latest league.

It has been revealed that ‘For example, how would a defender in Japan’s J1 League perform in the MLS in America? This kind of insight supports clubs to make smarter, more confident recruitment decisions across borders.’.

We’ll never know, of course, how different Celtic’s summer transfer dealings might have been had they got into bed with the manufacturer before this week.

But on one question, in particular, the Parkhead club would have been likely to have seen more red flags raised than a communist parade.

‘How would a forward who’s so clearly tailor-made for a unique environment north of the Arctic circle fare in the Scottish Premiership?’ Well, not too great, as it turns out.

Hogh endured another tough night in Portugal as his goalless run extended to 17 games.

Listen, you didn’t need to have a PhD in mathematics to question the wisdom of Celtic paying a record £11million to sign Kasper Hogh from Bodo/Glimt in the summer. Just an appreciation that so many players who’ve thrived at that extraordinary club have found success hard to come by elsewhere.

In a recent development, this observation is hardly new. It’s been the subject of discussions throughout Europe since the impressive Kjetil Knutsen began establishing a culture at the Norwegian outpost in 2018, one which would pave the way to four titles, a cup and a run to the semi-finals of the Europa League.

Knutsen and his sizeable entourage have created a world of their own 520 miles north of Oslo. And the dogs in the street know that those who venture outside it rarely do well.

According to recent reports, sure, Victor Boniface, now of Bayer Leverkusen, hasn’t really looked back since leaving for Union Saint-Gilloise. And Hugo Vetlesen has done well since moving to Club Brugge two years ago.

Sources indicate that but they are outnumbered by those who looked lost the minute Bodo/Glimt sold them. Patrick Berg, Fredrik Bjorkan and Jens Petter Hauge, to name but three.

Sources indicate that were Celtic not aware of this curious trend as Bodo/Glimt somehow convinced them to part with a club-record fee? Or did their research only go as far as the five goals Hogh scored in the Champions League last season?

Provided this Tuesday’s annual general meeting does not descend into disarray, an explanation from someone involved in the deal would be fitting.

In a recent development, hogh wasn’t some six-figure punt, after all. He was an eight-figure sure thing. Or, at least, that’s what the Celtic hierarchy believed him to be.

Who first flagged him up and who agreed that he was worthy of such a gargantuan investment? The trouble with Celtic these days is that no one is quite sure about who’s responsible for that kind of thing.

Recent findings suggest that despite Paul Tisdale leaving his head of football operations post on January 5, the club has yet to appoint a replacement. Nor has the vacant role been reclassified to that of director of football or sporting director.

Sources indicate that two months previously, chief scout Jay Lefevre left for Swansea. Despite Mark Cooper effectively filling that void and former Chelsea operative James Bell-Walker joining the team in January, officially, there is still no head of recruitment.

O'Neill turned to Columbian hitman Duran to get Celtic out of a hole against Torreense.

That’s just not a good look when the collective decision in June was to go all-in on a player who’s now gone 17 games without a goal.

Industry observers note that celtic’s partnership with the analytics company is all well and good and may indeed sharpen up the club’s future recruitment. It certainly needs it.

But it can’t undo what’s already done. And until such time as the club can cut its losses on Hogh and sign a replacement, Martin O’Neill has a serious problem on his hands.

Starting at Tynecastle tomorrow and up to the visit to Ibrox on January 3, Celtic have eight games to play.

That run includes a trip to Cyprus to face Omonia Nicosia, which now carries added significance after Thursday’s narrow win over Torreense revived the club’s Europa League hopes.

In a recent development, the trouble is that Hogh can no longer be trusted to deliver in any of those crucial matches. That much became abundantly clear across his dismal 59-minute contribution in Portugal.

That old cliché about strikers always being judged on goals has never actually rang true. Provided they hold the ball up and facilitate their team-mates to score, there will always be a degree of forgiveness.

Industry observers note that hogh’s epic goalless run stretching back to the hat-trick he hit at Kilmarnock on August 9 is only one part of the story now. It’s his inability to do the fundamentals of football — securing possession and finding a man — which have taken him to the point of no return.

In a recent development, this is no longer about one man needing a scruffy goal to get going. That’s just not going to happen. He’s demonstrably the wrong fit for Celtic. He has been a scandalous waste of money.

His display against Torreense was that of a player who is getting worse by the week, not better. He touched the ball just 13 times, misplaced three passes and only found a team-mate on seven occasions.

It has been revealed that hogh’s one moment of promise came when he robbed veteran defender Stopira in the right channel just before half-time. Having done the hard part and got to the line, his cut-back went straight into the goalkeeper’s arms.

Hogh's confidence already looks shot after making a miserable start to his Celtic career.

It has been revealed that ‘It’s poor. It’s really poor. He is really lacking conviction,’ stated former Celtic manager Neil Lennon.

It has been revealed that hogh’s withdrawal came not a moment too soon for the visiting fans. With approximately half as much time on the pitch, his replacement, Camilo Duran, managed just one touch fewer than the Dane, including the header for the winning goal which came from James Forrest’s cross.

Recent findings suggest that now with 15 goals for the season after signing from Qarabag for an initial £4.5m, the Colombian is continuing to prove that spending money is one thing. It’s how you spend it which is crucial.

O’Neill is hardly without options across the front area as a defining spell begins in Gorgie.

Industry observers note that after being sidelined for 18 months with a serious knee injury, Jota’s display against Torreense was scintillating. There should be no concerns now over the £8m which was spent to bring him back to the club.

Recent findings suggest that while Yang Hyun-jun had a poor night in Portugal, it was a rarity in recent times. The Korean is a different animal to the one which arrived from Gangwon FC three years back for £2.2m.

Recent findings suggest that haissem Hassan, Yang’s main rival on the right, hasn’t kicked a ball in Celtic’s last three matches. The fact that Forrest and Seb Tounekti stepped off the bench on Thursday before the £6m Egyptian was instructive.

Intriguingly, Callum Osmand remained there throughout. It won’t have escaped anyone’s notice that the 20-year-old arrived from Fulham ostensibly as a centre-forward.

He was recently afforded opportunities on the wing as Jota got back up to speed, but with the Portuguese returning to top form, that door is closing.

Osmand shouldn’t lose much sleep over that recent development, though. Without even shedding his tracksuit in Leiria, he jumped ahead of the hapless Hogh in the pecking order.

Tech Report: London’s people-first approach to smart-city development

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A virtual-reality model of London’s main financial district, the City of London, has mapped the size and location of every building.Credit: Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images.
  • London has risen to fourth place in the IMD Smart City Index 2026, up from sixth place in 2025 and eighth place in 2024.
  • “We increasingly describe our work as ‘city innovation’ rather than ‘smart cities’, because in many people’s minds ‘smart’ is associated with gadgets and gizmos,” states Dorling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A virtual-reality model of London’s main financial district, the City of London, has mapped the size and location of every building.Credit: Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images.

London has risen to fourth place in the IMD Smart City Index 2026, up from sixth place in 2025 and eighth place in 2024. The index — which is published by IMD, an independent Swiss business institute — draws mostly on residents’ perceptions of infrastructure and technology, not a tally of sensors. That focus on perspective is crucial, says Trevor Dorling, managing director of DG Cities, a private urban-innovation consultancy spun out of the Royal Borough of Greenwich local authority, which works to make better use of data and introduce fresh technologies in the southeast London borough.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

“We increasingly describe our work as ‘city innovation’ rather than ‘smart cities’, because in many people’s minds ‘smart’ is associated with gadgets and gizmos,” states Dorling. “The aim is to use technology to create better places for people. It shouldn’t be the technologists who define what ‘better’ is, but the communities that live there.”.

Recent findings suggest that there is plenty of evidence that London has the resources and knowledge to apply research solutions in such a people-centred way. In the 2026 Nature Index Science Cities table, London is ranked 21st overall, but it jumps to 5th place for health-sciences output, for instance.

The Smart Mobility Living Lab, created by a consortium of public and private organizations, including DG Cities, spans 24 kilometres of roads in Greenwich and the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford, and is one example of London’s efforts to create societal impact with its innovation.

Industry observers note that the area has more than 1,000 different road features, from speed bumps and pedestrian crossings to one-way systems and bridges, that allow companies to test fresh vehicles and services in busy, real-world complexity. “The driving force for this was the rapid development of self-driving technologies and exploring the opportunities this presented for safety and accessibility, as well as the challenges,” says Dorling.

Trials to test self-driving shuttle buses and delivery vans have put the technology in public view, with residents invited to ride in the test vehicles, an openness that Dorling says has helped overcome scepticism and brought local authorities into the development process at an early stage.

According to recent reports, london’s digital-twin projects are similarly pragmatic. The local authority in Harrow (northwest London) uses high-resolution drone imagery to inspect and measure roofs and buildings remotely and to build interactive maps of parks. The council used this approach in April 2026 to make a 3D model of Headstone Manor and Museum — a restored medieval complex and local-history museum — saving £12,000 (US$16,260) by avoiding a conventional roof survey with scaffolding and manual inspections.

In London’s main financial district, known as the City of London, a virtual-reality model created by the local authority in collaboration with researchers and digital spatial mappers has captured the size and location of every building, window, lamppost and traffic light within the area to within two centimetres of accuracy, allowing planners and the public to properly scrutinize building proposals.

Elsa Arcaute, a complexity science researcher at University College London, cautions against too much faith in digital twins, as a city with all its complexity and interplay between urbanity, nature and human behaviour cannot be completely duplicated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.

Industry observers note that the case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven.".

Sources indicate that as Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected.".

However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.

According to recent reports, "What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.

According to recent reports, however, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights.".

In a recent development, zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.

It has been revealed that "That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he noted.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.

Zverev's lawyers reject the allegations.

Sources indicate that "Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.

"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view.".

The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press.".

Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.

"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he mentioned. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.

"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice.".

Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League group stage match between RB Leipzig and Manchester City from Saxony. The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

According to recent reports, city, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

According to recent reports, for all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

In a recent development, the Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

The organization's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.

This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic is the first massive AI manufacturer to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI,  has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.

Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.

According to recent reports, anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.

That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.
  • The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
  • This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating complications such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.

This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating complications such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.

The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey.

It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.

According to recent reports, the draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, stated negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.

Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.

"This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he said in a statement.

According to recent reports, another hotly contested issue at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.

According to recent reports, the second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries. It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world.".

"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," remarked Raman.

The European Union has noted it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.

It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.".

Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen mentioned the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand.".

The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.

The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries mentioned the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community.".

The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.

Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.

On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demands for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate methane.

The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, noted Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

Australian Energy Minister Bowen stated he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.

"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a strategy we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming.".

The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

The conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.

Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such as Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.

"It's critically important for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," remarked David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

  • It has been revealed that helsinki’s technical prowess in these kinds of projects is underpinned by a substantial research base; the city is ranked 100th among the world’s top 200 cities in the Nature Index, with particular strength in health sciences (ranked 69th), biological sciences (80th) and Earth and environmental sciences (83rd).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Helsinki Central Library Oodi is just one example of a building in the Finnish capital that uses real-time data to optimize energy efficiency.Credit: Sergei Gapon/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images.

Urban planners — and curious residents — can go online and click on almost any building in Helsinki to see a host of details including its age, height, heating source and estimated energy use. The information sits in the various maps that make up Helsinki 3D, an open-data digital twin of the city built by the City of Helsinki from aerial photographs, light and detection laser scanning (LiDAR) surveys, housing registers and geographical data. The project’s Energy and Climate Atlas estimates heating demand for nearly every building, models how it would change in response to different climate conditions and calculates the solar-panel potential across every roof and wall in the Finnish capital.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

It has been revealed that helsinki’s technical prowess in these kinds of projects is underpinned by a substantial research base; the city is ranked 100th among the world’s top 200 cities in the Nature Index, with particular strength in health sciences (ranked 69th), biological sciences (80th) and Earth and environmental sciences (83rd). It produced 55% of Finland’s total Share in 2025, a ratio that is among the highest for cities in the overall top 200.

It has been revealed that the city has treated itself as a laboratory, too. Kalasatama, a brownfield site in the harbour district of Helsinki, has been designated as an urban testbed for researchers, city officials and companies to try out novel urban infrastructure ideas.

Recent findings suggest that helsinki’s Nordic climate is also an advantage when it comes to handling the large amounts of data involved with smart cities. Cooler air reduces the energy needed to chill large data centres and the excess warmth created by such facilities is redirected to residents using heat pumps. One of the largest data-centre operators that publishes its waste heat recovery data says it recovers up to 90% of its waste heat, which is fed into the district heating network — enough to warm 14,000 two-room apartments.

One of Helsinki’s most distinct smart-city features is the way it uses data.

Industry observers note that “We have to be responsible when we use AI. We must do it in a transparent way,” states Pasi Rautio, a service manager for the City of Helsinki’s AI and optimization unit.

The city’s AI register, for example, allows residents to keep tabs on AI projects the city’s government is running. It shows what data are being used and why, and offers the opportunity for public feedback.

#151815. Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky.
  • Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine.
  • In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he indicates, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine notes the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult.".

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Sources indicate that local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

In a recent development, "Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he mentioned.

Industry observers note that kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he mentioned, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," noted Popovych.

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff declared that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

According to recent reports, kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers presently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

In a recent development, the human rights activist mentioned that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 15:17 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 15:17 EST, 27 November 2026.

If Clydebank aren’t careful, getting the better of SPFL opposition will soon become something of an expectation rather than a hope. Then again, given their lofty ambitions, that’s exactly the kind of club they want to be.

It’s been 23 extraordinary years since its reformation, having gone bust following a series of events which left one of Scottish football’s great clubs — and great communities, for that matter — on its knees.

That it has taken less than a quarter of a century to get back within touching distance of the SPFL frankly beggars’ belief.

Win the Lowland League West — they right now sit three points behind leaders Largs Thistle with a couple of games in hand — and they will have a crack at earning promotion to the major time via a play-off.

Yet, as exciting a prospect as that may be, it’s something which will be a million miles from the minds of the players, staff and supporters as they rock up at Holm Park this afternoon for a Scottish Cup third-round clash against Championship high-flyers Livingston.

According to recent reports, this, of course, is not uncharted territory. Indeed, it’s the third time in as many years that the club have made it to this stage of the competition, and even made it one round further in 2024-25 before bowing out to Hibs at Easter Road.

Clydebank will welcome Championship side Livingston to Holm Park tomorrow.

Yet it wouldn’t necessarily be a great surprise if they were to reach that stage again this time around given the way in which they’ve gone about their business with such professionalism against teams playing much higher up in the football pyramid.

Their incredible run to the KDM Evolution Trophy quarter-finals saw them defeat Dumbarton, East Fife, Kelty Hearts and Alloa Athletic before progressing on penalties against Queen’s Park on Tuesday night.

That win marked the 77th consecutive domestic match in which Clydebank have found the net, incidentally, having surpassed Celtic’s record of 75 set in 2017 a few days earlier.

Pulling off a shock once, maybe even twice, could be put down to luck. To do so habitually is something different. Which is why this is a bit of a nightmare draw for Livi.

The days of non-league clubs simply making up the numbers at this point of the competition are a thing of the past, with the gap between the second and fifth tiers of Scottish football seemingly getting smaller with each passing year.

That the likes of Clydebank will genuinely believe they can beat a team chasing an immediate return to the top flight suggests as much.

They are not the only Lowland League West side in action today, with Cumnock Juniors eyeing up a shock as they welcome Championship outfit Arbroath, who know a thing or two about upsetting the odds having punched well above their weight for long enough.

You suspect Raith Rovers won’t be relishing their journey to face Troon at Portland Park, a stadium perhaps best known for hosting a few Brazilian chaps including Pele, Garrincha, Tostao and Zico ahead of the 1966 World Cup in England.

The Lowland League West side have beaten the likes of Alloa and Queen's Park this season.

The names of today’s visitors may not quite carry the same gravitas, but nevertheless, it’s arguably the biggest game in Troon’s 80-year history.

One thing is for certain: there will be at least one Lowland League West club in the hat for the next round, with Renfrew — who have Argyll McCoist, son of Rangers legend Ally in their squad — going head-to-head with Cumbernauld Colts, with both chasing a money-spinning fourth-round tie against one of the country’s big guns.

Bo’ness United and Brechin City — both battling it out in the Lowland League East this season — are in the same boat ahead of their meeting at Newton Park.

Fifty miles separate Ross County and Brora Rangers ahead of their clash in Dingwall, but in Highland terms, it constitutes something of a derby.

The visitors are looking to follow in their opponents footsteps by getting up to the SPFL this season, 22 years after County broke through. And they are going about it the right way too, having gone unbeaten in the Highland League so far this term.

Funnily enough, they are coming against the only other team in Scotland’s top five tiers who share that particular accolade.

And those in charge at Morton will be praying their side can survive their trip to League Two’s basement side Annan Athletic in the hope of pulling a lucrative fixture in the next round.

Amid all the financial uncertainty and concern regarding the future of the Cappielow club these days — even more so following the news earlier this week that main sponsor Dalrada Technology Ltd has been placed in liquidation — goodness knows they need some positivity around the place.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

England head coach Thomas Tuchel described his relationship with Jude Bellingham as being “in a good place” after admitting it had been “a bit up and down”.

Tuchel has two Bellinghams in his latest England squad after calling up Jude’s brother, Jobe, for the first time for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. If they play together, it will be the first time brothers have represented England in the same team since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago.

This time last year, Tuchel cast doubt over Jude’s place in his team by picking Morgan Rogers over him, having not included the Real Madrid midfielder in an England squad the previous month.

But Jude performed superbly for Tuchel at the World Cup and was England’s best player during the last international camp. Tuchel revealed he has listened to his advice by calling up 21-year-old Jobe.

Asked if his relationship with Jude has developed, Tuchel stated: “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course, but we are in a good place.

“I love to be his coach, he’s a top player, a very influential player and it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable, he would not perform at that level.

Sources indicate that “At the moment, you see he’s happy to come into camp, he’s happy with the role he has, he’s fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them [Bellingham brothers] is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach.”.

Jobe has captained England’s Under-21s and, as well as U21 head coach Lee Carlsey, Tuchel acknowledged the influence of Jude on the Borussia Dortmund midfielder’s first senior call.

Jude once said that playing with Jobe for England would be “the biggest dream of my life” and that it would mean more to him than any trophies.

Discussing Jude’s influence on Jobe’s selection, Tuchel said: “We spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream and Jude was always like, ‘Watch him, he’s good, he can make it,’ I would say, ‘Yeah we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, from Lee Carsley and we see him with the Under-21s and there is such positive feedback.

“This is also the signal that if you are good in the Under-21s, this is the next step. We had it with Elliot Anderson, we had it with Alex Scott, we have it with Jarell Quansah and it counts. If you play good for England in the Under-19s, 20s, 21s, if you play good for England in tournaments then it means something.”.

According to recent reports, tuchel at one point had to correct himself, with a laugh, when he accidentally referred to Jobe as Jube. On the subject of how Jobe reacted to his call-up and the comparisons with his brother that he will inevitably face, Tuchel mentioned: “He has to live with this that everyone will compare them. They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. And let’s see – they are also different characters, at least that’s what I heard.

Recent findings suggest that “He [Jobe] watched training very early in my [reign]. In my first March camp maybe, he came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and we said, ‘Ah, it would be nice if one day you are with him [Jude].’ He was very kind and polite and I’m glad to have him in camp.

Industry observers note that “He couldn’t stop smiling [when I told him]. He has the same beautiful smile as Jude, so it’s nice to have him. Let’s see what the effect is. What I saw, Jude was always the major brother that you imagine, taking care of his younger brother and making sure everything is alright. Behaving like a big brother. And that helps Jobe now. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close and in camp and to have this experience together. It’s a very special moment for them.”.

The room is furnished in a typical Austrian style. Lots of wood, a fireplace, a few decorative touches. Through the large windows, you can see mountains surrounding the town of Saalfelden. Right on the dot, 21-year-old Jobe Bellingham arrives. It is August 2025, the midfielder has just signed for Borussia Dortmund and is giving his first press conference at the club’s training camp. German journalists are eager to find out what kind of character this talented youngster is. Will he provide any useful quotes for a story?

It has been revealed that half an hour later, the reporters are full of admiration and their notepads are full. Open-minded, self-assured, with clear opinions and a firm stance. That is how Bellingham presents himself. “It’s just not in my nature to be a superstar. I want to function like a machine,” he indicates. That was 15 months ago – a lot has happened since.

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

Industry observers note that the problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

Ever since, the midfielder has enjoyed almost unwavering support. Watzke frequently spoke with him throughout his first season, offering encouragement and reassurance. Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment.
  • Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply.
  • "We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now claims overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

Industry observers note that "It feels like your eyes are burning," mentioned Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven.".

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, indicates Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she stated.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.

The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors noted.

In a recent development, failure to cut emissions rapidly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today.".

Recent findings suggest that he points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in latest renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy aims focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International claims they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system.".

In a recent development, france is sticking to a previously revealed deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

Industry observers note that "None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan.".

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she stated. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

By harnessing potent antibodies that can vanquish diverse viral strains, scientists are closing in on one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine for HIV. This year, several research teams described vaccination strategies that triggered the production of these broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) in monkeys, and precursors to bnAbs in people, suggesting that an effective vaccine is possible. But devastating cuts to US funding for HIV research have left some efforts in limbo.

In a recent development, the world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine. It also has a drug capable of preventing infections: the long-acting injectable drug lenacapavir, which could avert an estimated one-third of new HIV infections in Africa if given to just 5% of adults. Now is the time for funders to ramp up investment, not cut it back, argues a Nature editorial.

Reference: UNAIDS & Gates Foundation report.

Pregnancy causes drastic changes to the brain, but we know little about them because of past worries about the safety of scanning pregnant people. Now, researchers are working to fill that void by collecting scans from first- and second-time mothers and analysing thousands of archived brain scans acquired during routine clinical care. The work, presented last week at the US Society for Neuroscience annual meeting, could help to explain maternal mental-health conditions such as postpartum depression.

It has been revealed that ‘General purpose’ artificial-intelligence tools such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude are impressing researchers with their emerging biology skills, including protein design and structure prediction. In some tests, these models have even outperformed those designed specifically for biology tasks and trained on vast troves of protein-sequence data. Some scientists predict that generalist AI tools could eventually catch up with, or surpass, blockbuster models such as AlphaFold. Others suggest these new abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data, rather than advanced learning.

As I write, the United States army is preparing to detonate around 4.4 tonnes of unstable lead azide, a chemical used to make munitions, at an ammunition plant in Iowa. “It's essentially a lead bomb,” says occupational and environmental health researcher Patrick O’Shaughnessy. “Now it's a matter of how much gets ejected out of the bunker.” Academic researchers have banded together to gather independent public data about the plume of toxic lead dust that is expected to spread over the area.

Figure 1 | Position verification. a, To check the location of a party called the prover, two verifiers each send a random bit (a challenge), which are timed to reach the location simultaneously. The prover combines the bits and returns the answer. Because no signal travels faster than light, a prompt reply shows that the prover is at the location. b, However, if two adversaries, one near each verifier, copy a challenge and pass it to each other, they can answer in time even though nobody is at the claimed location. c, In Kavuri and colleagues’ scheme, one verifier generates two entangled photons, keeping one and sending the other to the prover. Both verifiers then transmit classical challenges. The prover uses the challenges to determine how to measure its photon and returns the result, while the first verifier measures the other photon. If the prover’s result arrives in time and the two measurements pass a statistical check (a Bell test), the transmitted photon must have been measured at the claimed location.

“Banks, power grids and satellite-navigation systems all depend on knowing where a request or a signal comes from, yet claims about location are notoriously easy to fake,” notes physicist Davide Bacco. Now researchers have outlined an experiment in which the position of a distant party is certified using quantum entanglement.

It has been revealed that in a, two verifiers send random bits (challenges) timed to reach the claimed location simultaneously. The prover combines them and replies. Because signals cannot travel faster than light, a prompt response verifies the prover’s location. But two adversaries (b) can defeat this test by exchanging the challenges and responding in time. In (c), a verifier also sends one of two entangled photons, which are inexorably linked in a way that can be proven using a statistical check (a Bell test). If the prover’s result arrives inside the time window imposed by the speed of light and the photons pass the Bell test, the prover must be inside the target region. (Nature | 9 min read).

According to recent reports, chemist George Whitesides made landmark contributions to many fields, including patterning surfaces with molecules — a technique that enabled ‘lab on a chip’ diagnostic devices — advances in nanotechnology and more. He prided himself on switching research interests often, telling students, “If somebody else is working on something, don’t work on it.” In traditional chemistry departments, “there’s often a lot of pressure to stay in your lane, and he made it okay not to”, says polymer scientist Joseph DeSimone. “In fact, he made it exciting not to.” Whitesides has died, aged 87.

Read Whitesides’s guide to writing a scientific paper in a special glitch of Advanced Materials that celebrated his 65th birthday.

Some mental disorders seem to take different forms in different places, writes mental-illness researcher Alexander Pereira. “Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears,” he writes — with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, prevalent in China, and psychological symptoms, such as low self-esteem, more common in the West. Pereira argues that our ability to adapt to our social environment might significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental health.

Changing location — even just walking through a doorway — can signal to our brains that work is over and it’s time to relax, indicates cognitive scientist Joan Ongchoco. (BBC Future | 11 min read).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a organization letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.

According to recent reports, this is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful.".

"Lufthansa is presently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter remarked.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

The company also looks to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Industry observers note that furthermore, it intends to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.

The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously confirmed downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa stated it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hill Dickinson Stadium welcomed some of Liverpool’s care experienced young people for an exclusive behind-the-scenes tour to mark National Care Leavers Month. A group of 25 care leavers, who have either left or are preparing to leave local authority care, were given the opportunity to explore the Club’s stunning waterfront home. Observed every November, National Care Leavers Month is a UK-wide campaign that celebrates care experienced young people, amplifies their voices and promotes positive change in policy and practice. The youngsters, many of whom were visiting a football stadium for the first time, enjoyed an informative tour of the state-of-the-art venue, including the impressive home dressing room, the Media Centre, pitchside areas and learning about the heritage of the historic site. Jenny Glennard, Corporate Director of Children & Young People’s Services at Liverpool City Council, said: "On behalf of Liverpool Children's Social Care, I would like to again extend my gratitude to Everton for providing our care experienced young people with the fantastic opportunity to visit Hill Dickinson Stadium as part of National Care Leavers Month. "To be given a personal group tour was an experience and memory they will never forget. All of our young people have expressed how much they enjoyed the day and how impressed they were with the stadium, as well as the staff who made them feel so welcome. "We value our relationship with Everton and look forward to continuing to work with the Club in the future." Liverpool City Council's Leaving Care Services provide a wide range of support for young people transitioning from local authority care. Using a person-centred approach to independent living skills, planning and assessment, the service aims to improve outcomes across education, training, employment, health and accommodation. Everton has confirmed a newly introduced multi-year partnership with global power technology brand NOCO.

The agreement will see the US-headquartered company become Everton’s 'Official Battery Charging Partner', further strengthening the Club’s growing portfolio of international commercial partners.

Founded in Cleveland, Ohio in 1914, NOCO has established itself as an internationally-recognised name in power technology, specialising in battery chargers, portable jump starters, tyre inflators, lithium batteries and related accessories.

With more than 110 years of innovation behind it, the company has developed a significant international presence, with offices and operations spanning North America, Europe, Asia and Australia.

As part of the partnership, NOCO will benefit from prominent brand visibility across Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, with LED perimeter advertising and exposure through the Club’s digital and social media channels.

The agreement will also provide NOCO with opportunities to host international clients and business guests and events at Everton fixtures at Hill Dickinson Stadium, using the Club’s matchday experiences to develop relationships and support its global business network.

Mark Rollings, Chief Partnerships Officer at Everton, said: “We are delighted to welcome NOCO to Everton.

“NOCO is a well-established and respected international business with a proud heritage, a strong reputation for innovation and clear ambitions for continued global growth.

“Securing a brand of NOCO’s standing in a new commercial category is another positive step in the development of our partnership portfolio. It also demonstrates Everton’s growing profile and the opportunities we can offer international businesses looking to build their brand through the global reach of the Premier League.

“NOCO joins an impressive group of globally recognised businesses already working with Everton, and we look forward to building a successful relationship that supports its continued growth.”.

The partnership comes at a time of continued international expansion for NOCO, which has strengthened its presence in key overseas markets, including a recent agreement with AUTOBACS Global, one of Japan’s leading automotive retailers.

NOCO was also recently recognised at the 2026 Circana Automotive Aftermarket Performance Awards, winning the Maintenance & Repair category for achieving the highest increase in US market share.

Zachary Koehler, Partnership Marketing Manager at NOCO, stated: We’re proud to partner with Everton, a club with a rich history and one of the most passionate fanbases in world football.

According to recent reports, “Like Everton, NOCO is built on more than a century of heritage and a drive to keep moving forward. As we continue to grow internationally, the global reach of the Premier League gives us a powerful platform to connect with new audiences, customers, and partners.

“We can’t think of a better way to make our debut than the Merseyside derby, and we look forward to a successful partnership with everyone at Everton.".

The agreement will see NOCO branding formally make its debut at Everton’s next home fixture, the Merseyside derby, and further underlines the Club’s growing commercial momentum and international appeal. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 member nations of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027.
  • According to recent reports, gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 member nations of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.

According to recent reports, gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under Infantino's leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.

During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia — a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.

Industry observers note that at the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.

In a recent development, infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate — whether exemplified by his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly after the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.

Industry observers note that A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has also placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment proposal, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.

Sources indicate that philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.

He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).

"Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf mentioned in a statement announcing the German FA's position.

"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction.".

Sources indicate that diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.

Recent findings suggest that the third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.

During a press conference in the Japanese capital Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.

"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he noted.

"Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization.".

Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations — the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino — makes him a longshot to win the election.

In a recent development, but he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.

"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," he stated.

"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.

However, Tashima also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.

If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

According to recent reports, daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

They never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

In a recent development, spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.
